title: I’m losing every new player in my mobile strategy game’s tutorial. How do you balance “basic rules” vs “the subtle stuff”?
author: Infinite-One-9078
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I’m working on the tutorial for my game, Falltasy, and it’s harder than I expected. It’s a mobile game, but it’s fairly strategic. So I keep going back and forth between teaching just the basic rules and explaining all the subtleties that make the game interesting.

Right now I’m losing pretty much every new player, so I know my approach needs a rethink.

A few questions for those who’ve been through this:

* Do you teach everything up front, or let players discover the depth over several runs?
* Have you had better results with short rule screens, scripted first levels, or contextual tips that show up when they matter?
* How do you tell whether players leave because of the tutorial or because of the game itself?

*(AI side: the game is built with Claude Code, and the sprites/backgrounds are made with Midjourney + a custom cleanup pipeline. Happy to talk about that too.)*

If you want to try the first-play tutorial and tell me where you got lost or bored, here’s the link: [**https://madmanu77.itch.io/falltasy**](https://madmanu77.itch.io/falltasy)

Thanks a lot!

comments.author: UnderLord7985
comments.body: I believe players need to learn the game on the first go if not you'll lose players left and right, you dont need to teach them everything at the start, but the basics to get going are the main focus in the first 15 minutes of game play and as they dive deeper into the game you introduce the deeper mechanics. But teaching them everythimg from the get go can feel overwhelming.

replies.author: Infinite-One-9078
replies.body: I agree. The balance is not easy to set up about complexity and quicky play. Some tips?

replies.author: UnderLord7985
replies.body: My tip is to start with the basic game play i dont know what your game is about, but how i would figure out what to do and in what order to do it is create a flow chart learning to move flows into atacking, attackimg flows into parrying or using defenses so on and so forth until you have a flow chart with all the basics down, then you break the flow chart down into sections for each attack defense, trading etc to see how that leads into the deeper mechanics its gonna take some planning but a flow chart usually works for me because im very visual.

comments.author: No-Pollution7797
comments.body:
I'd answer your third question first, because it decides the other two. Put a simple event on each tutorial step and on the start of the first real match, then look at where people actually stop. If most of them quit on one specific screen it's the tutorial, but if they get through it and never start a second game, the problem is more likely the first match itself.

For a strategic game I'd teach only what you need to win the first fight, and make the first opponent easy enough that a sloppy player still wins. The subtle stuff lands much better as a short tip right after a loss, when the player already wants to know why it happened, than as a rule screen before they've played at all.

comments.author: lawlshawk
comments.body:
the step events idea above is the right one ... it's basically a funnel. tutorial start > each step > first real match > second match. the step with the biggest drop is your answer, and if they finish the tutorial but never start match 2 it's the game not the tutorial

  
for a strategy game i'd teach only what you need to win the first fight and drip the rest in as contextual tips when it actually comes up. long rule screens up front is where people bail imo

  
two things i've had in mine from day 0 that help here ... a short in-game survey (one question on quit like "what made you stop?" is cheap) and a simple replay engine for boss fights. watching what people actually do beats asking them, they'll rarely tell you they were confused
